Die Geschichte unserer Welt ist von ihren Konflikten geprägt worden. Von den frühesten Streitigkeiten Kains und Abels bis zu den militärischen Operationen des einundzwanzigsten Jahrhunderts hat die Menschheit nie aufgehört, einander anzugreifen. Friedenszeiten sind einfach Wartezeiten auf die nächste Schlacht; Verträge und Waffenstillstände sind nur Verzögerungen der Gewalt.

Die Kriege des geistlichen Reiches waren ebenso lang und ebenso brutal wie die physischen Kriege. Diese Kämpfe reichen zu uns zurück bis in die früheste Morgendämmerung der Zeit, wo sie in den Herzen Adams und Evas ihren Ursprung hatten. Der Kampf gegen Versuchung und Auflehnung ist in jedem von uns präsent, ob er nun anerkannt wird oder nicht. Nur wenige gehen siegreich in einen wahren Frieden hervor, und selbst dieser Frieden ist ein wachsamer Friede, der in einem Moment des Schwankens zerschmettert werden kann.

Der folgende Bericht ist nur ein kurzer Funke in diesem prüfenden Feuer des Streits.

Das Jahr war 1942, und überall auf der Welt tobte ein Krieg, wie man ihn zuvor noch nie gesehen hatte. Zerstörung und Blutvergießen waren zur Gewohnheit geworden, nirgends mehr als im Pazifikraum. Dort, gesprenkelt über die weite blaue Fläche des Pazifischen Ozeans, beherbergten die tropischen Inseln Schlachten von unvergleichlicher Heftigkeit und Grausamkeit. Selbstmordstürme, Artillerievernichtung und Luftangriffe machten das Leben des einfachen Soldaten zu einem lebenden Albtraum. Jederzeit konnte ein Banzai-Ansturm (ein typischerweise nächtlicher All-Out-Angriff massierter Infanterie, die auf dem Weg zum Angriff mit lauter Stimme schreit) die Nachtluft in einen Ansturm von angreifenden Feinden teilen, die in eine Tötungsraserei versetzt wurden. Eine fehlgeleitete Granate, einige so schwer wie ein kleines Auto, konnte aus dem Himmel fallen mit tödlichen Folgen. Der Tod war allgegenwärtig und forderte scheinbar zufällig Leben.

Viertausend Meilen östlich tobte ein anderer Kampf. Dieser war ebenso tödlich wie der erste und umfasste Hunderte junger Männer in einem Alles-umfassenden Kampf um ihr geistliches Überleben. Anstatt des physischen Kampfes auf den orientalischen Inseln des Fernen Ostens, würde dieser Kampf in den Herzen und Gedanken der an ihm Beteiligten ausgetragen werden. Statt Maschinengewehren und Granaten würden sie mit dem schärfsten zweischneidigen Schwert bewaffnet sein (die Heilige Schrift), geleitet von einer Macht (dem Heiligen Geist), die größer ist als jede Seeflotte.

Diese jungen Männer waren zu einem Dienstzeitraum in den physischen Kriegsanstrengungen berufen worden, die tobten. Zwei Jahre zuvor war der Selective Training and Service Act von 1940 verabschiedet worden, bevor die Vereinigten Staaten in den Krieg eingetreten waren. Dieses Gesetz verpflichtete alle Männer zwischen achtzehn und fünfundvierzig Jahren, sich für die Einberufung registrieren zu lassen. Die Ausgewählten sollten eine einjährige Dienstzeit ableisten. Sobald jedoch Krieg erklärt wurde, sollte diese Frist bis zum Ende der Kämpfe verlängert werden.

Bei diesen jungen Männern weckte diese Einberufung und der gegenwärtige Krieg Erinnerungen an Geschichten von einem ähnlichen Krieg und einer ähnlichen Einberufung, kaum eine Generation zuvor, die ihre Väter zu den Ausbildungslagern des US-Militärs gerufen hatte. Dort war die ältere Generation allerlei bösartiger Misshandlungen ausgesetzt gewesen. Damals wurde erwartet, dass alle kräftigen jungen Männer nicht nur willig, sondern auch eifrig sein würden, ihrem Land im Kampf gegen den Feind zu dienen. Diese vorherrschende Haltung hatte allgemein Ärger und Feindseligkeit gegenüber den Kriegsdienstgegnern des Ersten Weltkriegs hervorgerufen. Druck wurde ausgeübt, sie dazu zu bringen, sich an den Übungen und der Disziplin der Streitkräfte zu beteiligen, und verschiedene Strafen konnten gegen jene verhängt werden, die sich weigerten. So schwer waren die Strafen, dass viele körperlich litten und mehrere durch die Behandlung, die sie erhielten, getötet wurden.

Ähnlich wie ihre Väter wurden diese jungen Männer aufgerufen, ihrem irdischen Land durch das Ergreifen von Waffen zu dienen. Die Einberufenen sollten sich bei ihrem örtlichen Rekrutierungsbüro melden, wo sie organisiert und zu einem der mehreren Ausbildungslager im Land geschickt würden. Dort sollten sie zu Soldaten geformt, darauf vorbereitet werden, ihre Mitmenschen zu töten, und dann zu diesem Zweck ins Ausland geschickt werden. Doch ihr Glaube ordnete anderes an.

Glücklicherweise waren sie nicht die Einzigen, die sich an den Ersten Weltkrieg erinnerten. In den zweieinhalb Jahrzehnten seit diesem Krieg hatten sowohl Mennoniten als auch verschiedene besorgte Einzelpersonen daran gearbeitet sicherzustellen, dass, falls die Not eintreten sollte, eine Option vorhanden wäre, die den Anforderungen des Staates an den Dienst gerecht werden konnte, ohne gegen die Prinzipien und Überzeugungen der Kriegsdienstgegner zu verstoßen. So wurden verschiedene Organisationen und Programme ins Leben gerufen, die eine Befreiung vom Militärdienst ermöglichten. Kriegsdienstgegner wurden durch diese Programme in verschiedene Dienstrollen eingegliedert. Sie dienten in Krankenhäusern, bauten Straßen und Bewässerungskanäle und stellten Arbeitskraft für Naturschutzmaßnahmen bereit. Auf diese Weise konnten sie das Gesetz erfüllen, ohne das Gesetz zu brechen (siehe Markus 12,17).

Trotz der bürokratischen Anerkennung der Überzeugungen der Kriegsdienstgegner und ihres anschließenden Ersatzdienstes kochte die öffentliche Stimmung oft noch gegen nicht nur die gewaltfreien Mennoniten und Amish, sondern gegen jegliche Kriegsdienstgegner. Personen, die sich weigerten zu kämpfen, konnten erwarten, dass nicht nur sie persönlich unter Druck gesetzt würden, sondern dass auch ihre Familien und Freunde unter Beobachtung gerieten. Einige ihrer Familien wurden gemieden oder herabgesetzt, die lokale Gemeinschaft boykottierte ihre Geschäfte. In einigen Fällen schauten örtliche Behörden bei Misshandlungen gewaltfreier Menschen in ihrem Zuständigkeitsbereich weg. In extremen Fällen kochte der Patriotismus über und führte zu Mobs, Sachschäden und in wenigen seltenen Fällen zu direkten Angriffen gegen die wahrgenommenen Drückeberger.

Obwohl die meisten Teile Europas und seine Verbündeten seit Hitlers Invasion in Polen im September 1939 in diesen Krieg verwickelt gewesen waren, trat die Vereinigten Staaten nicht in die anfängliche Auseinandersetzung ein. Während die deutsche Armee durch Europa stürmte, dominierten in den frühen Jahren des Pazifikkriegs die Japaner, die bereits 1937 in China eingefallen waren. Die Vereinigten Staaten blieben in dieser Zeit neutral, getrieben von einem allgemeinen Gefühl des Isolationismus. All dies änderte sich am Morgen des 7. Dezember 1941, als die japanische Marine einen Überraschungsangriff auf die Vereinigten Staaten startete und Schiffe im Hafen von Pearl Harbor angriff, dem Heimathafen der US-Pazifikflotte. Die Vergeltung war schnell, und es wurde Krieg gegen Japan und seine Verbündeten erklärt. Japan verdoppelte seine Offensive und fegte über die im Pazifik verstreuten Inselstaaten hinweg. Das japanische Engagement für den Krieg war persönlich und intensiv. Ehre, selbst in der Todesstunde, wurde höher geschätzt als das Leben. Der Kaiser wurde als unfehlbar verehrt, und japanische Soldaten stürzten sich in seinem Namen in den Kampf, selbst angesichts überwältigender Chancen. Angetrieben von seinem Fanatismus und einer effizienten, gut versorgten Angriffskraft, richtete Japan seinen Blick auf die Philippinen. Dort traf seine Armee auf eine Streitmacht, die ihnen weit unterlegen war.

Unterdessen standen an ihren verschiedenen Stationen im ganzen Land die Kriegsdienstgegner vor ihrem eigenen Angriff. Ihnen war die Erleichterung gewährt worden, keinen physischen Kampf führen zu müssen. Mit dieser Ausnahme eröffneten sich aber ungeahnte Möglichkeiten, den leidenden Personen in ihrer Obhut zu dienen. In ihren verschiedenen Diensten begegneten sie allen möglichen Menschen. Jede Begegnung war eine weitere Möglichkeit, den Frieden und die Liebe eines Christen mitten im anhaltenden Krieg zu zeigen, besonders in den psychiatrischen Einrichtungen und Krankenhäusern, die einige der Kriegsdienstgegner beschäftigten. Der Zustand der Psychiatrien war damals beklagenswert. Patienten wurden grob behandelt oder einfach vernachlässigt. Schwierige Patienten wurden wochenlang in Zwangsjacken gebunden oder gezwungen, in ihrem eigenen Unrat zu leben. Ernährung und Hygiene reichten bei weitem nicht aus, um den vorhandenen Bedarf zu decken. Mehrere der jungen Männer machten durch Briefe an Zeitungen oder durch Schilderung ihrer Beobachtungen über den Missbrauch gegenüber ihren Kontakten zu Hause auf die Situation der geistig Behinderten aufmerksam. Diese Aktionen führten zu wachsendem öffentlichen Bewusstsein und Besorgnis über die Behandlung der Behinderten, was der Auslöser für Veränderungen in der Pflege derjenigen war, die sich nicht selbst versorgen konnten.

Leider kam die Gelegenheit zu dienen zu einem Preis. Die Kriegsdienstgegner waren jung und von ihrer Kirche und Familie getrennt. Ungöttliche Einflüsse wimmelten um sie herum. Weil sie von ihren Gemeinden und Familien getrennt waren, wogen diese Einflüsse schwerer auf den Gedanken der jungen Männer, als sie es zu Hause getan hätten. Der Kampf tobte weiter, und nun mehr denn je mussten sie sich auf Gott als ihre Stärke, Stütze und Verteidigung stützen.

Im Pazifik rüstete Japan zu einem überwältigenden Angriff auf die Philippinen. Die Inselnation hatte lange ihre Verteidigung vorbereitet, und nun würde sie durch den Vorstoß der japanischen Eindringlinge geprüft werden. Diese verteidigende Armee war ein Produkt der Ausbildung und Führung General George A. MacArthurs. MacArthur war gewissermaßen ein Wunderkind des US-Militärs und hatte sich aus seinem Dienst im Ersten Weltkrieg als jüngster Divisionär der Armee hervorgehoben. Seitdem hatte er seine Zeit zwischen den Kriegen weitgehend auf den Philippinen verbracht, deren Strände und Dschungel er nun verteidigte. In den Monaten vor der Invasion bat er um Verstärkung, modernere Ausrüstung und ausreichende Materialien, um einen Angriff aushalten zu können. Da der Fokus der Vereinigten Staaten damals darauf gerichtet war, zuerst den Krieg in Europa zu gewinnen, wurden seine Bitten abgelehnt, und er war daher unterbesetzt und unterbewaffnet. Dennoch grub sich MacArthur ein und bereitete sich darauf vor, gegen die unvermeidlichen Landungen und das anschließende Vordringen der Eindringlinge zu verteidigen. Seine Truppen erlitten massive Verluste bei ihrem langsamen Rückzug. Obwohl die Niederlage bald offensichtlich wurde, weigerte sich der General, die Insel zu verlassen. Erst als die Insel nahezu verloren war, ließ er sich überreden, feindliche Linien zu durchbrechen und nach Batchelor Field in Australien zu evakuieren. Dort gab er denen, die er zurückgelassen hatte, ein feierliches Versprechen: „I shall return.“

Die Kriegsdienstgegner, nun über zahlreiche Projekte und Einsatzfelder verteilt, sahen sich einer ebenso vielfältigen Reihe von Herausforderungen gegenüber. Anstatt der beständigen Leitung ihrer Heimatgemeinden standen sie nun unter der Führung staatlich bestellter Direktoren. Ihre Lagerpläne hielten sie bis zu sechs Tage die Woche auf Trab. Sonntage waren im Allgemeinen dem Gottesdienst vorbehalten. Der Einfluss einer von Krieg umgebenen Welt hatte sich durchgesetzt. Harry Litwiller, ein mennonitischer Jugendlicher in Kanada, war einer jener, die den weltlichen Einflüssen verfielen. Er war in die Armee eingereiht worden, wo er schnell den Status eines Kriegsdienstgegners beantragte. Während sein Antrag bearbeitet wurde, hatte er von anderen Rekruten das Glücksspiel und Trinken übernommen. Gerüchte über seine neuen Gewohnheiten gelangten bald zu seinen militärischen Vorgesetzten, und sein Antrag wurde abgelehnt. Kirchen beteten, schrieben Briefe und unternahmen sonstige Anstrengungen, um die jungen Männer in ihren Prüfungen zu unterstützen. Sie konnten es nicht wissen, aber ihre Zeit der Prüfung würde bald zu Ende gehen.

Endlich war das Jahr 1945 gekommen. Die letzten Monate des Krieges hatten die Einberufung junger Burschen und alter Männer in die deutsche Armee gesehen, als Hitler einen letzten verzweifelten Stand versuchte und zwischen den alliierten Armeen der Ost- und Westfront gefangen war. Unfähig weiterzumachen, baten die Deutschen um Frieden. Nun, da der Krieg in Europa vorbei war, verlagerte sich die Kriegstide auf den Pazifik. Amerika sammelte sich, angetrieben von seiner größeren industriellen Kapazität und seinen natürlichen Ressourcen, wodurch der japanische Vormarsch ins Stocken geriet—somit begann die amerikanische Gegenoffensive. Langsam, von Insel zu Insel überspringend, näherte sich General MacArthur Japan immer weiter an.

MacArthur hatte sein Versprechen gegenüber dem philippinischen Volk nicht vergessen. In seinen vier Jahren Abwesenheit waren Kämpfe um kleinste Atolle geführt worden—Koralleninseln, gerade groß genug für einen Flugplatz und eine Garnison. Selbst als die Japaner aus diesen Stützpunkten verdrängt wurden, behielten sie in den Philippinen noch festen Fuß. Die Inselnation hatte die Jahre der Feindbesetzung durchlitten. Sie beherbergte Gefangenenlager—Lager für Kriegsgefangene und solche, die der Unterstützung der Alliierten beschuldigt wurden.

Die Zeit lief nun gegen die Japaner. Dünn verteilt—mit schwindenden Truppen, Ausrüstung und Ressourcen—führten sie eine verzweifelte Verteidigungskampagne. Am 24. Oktober 1944 landete eine alliierte Streitmacht an der Ostküste der Insel Leyte. Die Schlacht um die Philippinen würde zwei Monate dauern, aber am Ende ging MacArthur als Sieger hervor. Viele Monate zuvor hatte er die Kapitulation der Insel überwacht, nun befahl er ihre Rückeroberung. Sein Versprechen wurde erfüllt.

Der Krieg zog sich hin. In Europa war er beendet, doch im Pazifik war er noch nicht gewonnen. Präsident Franklin D. Roosevelt, der die Nation durch den Krieg geführt hatte, erkrankte und starb. Sein Vizepräsident, Harry S. Truman, wurde vereidigt. Seine erste Entscheidung war eine, die er sich niemals hätte vorstellen können. Sollte er Hunderttausende Leben einsetzen, um Japan zu Fuß zu nehmen, oder sie zum grausamen Beispiel einer neu entwickelten Atombombe machen, die aus relativer Sicherheit der Lüfte abgeworfen würde? Truman beriet und traf seine Wahl.

Der Krieg endete im Handumdrehen. Die Verwüstung durch ein Paar Atombomben schockte Japan zur Kapitulation. Sie baten um Frieden, und Frieden wurde gewährt. Abgesehen von den Formalitäten war der Krieg zu Ende. Vorbei, aber der temporäre Frieden war mit einem astronomischen Preis an Menschenleben erkauft worden. Millionen kehrten nie zu ihren trauernden Familien zurück.

Für die Kriegsdienstgegner war es die Rückkehr zu einer neuen Normalität. Sie kehrten zu ihren Familien, ihren Kirchen und ihren Häusern zurück. Doch der Krieg hatte sie verändert. Monate und Jahre waren fern der geistlichen Aufsicht vergangen. Viele würden sich in ihren Gemeinden niederlassen, ihre Familien großziehen und ihren christlichen Glauben leben. Doch es hatte Verluste gegeben, einige, wie Harry Litwiller, hatten ihren Glauben aufgegeben. Der Kampf war heftig gewesen, und nicht alle seine Kämpfer hatten die volle biblische Waffenrüstung getragen, die ihnen zur Verfügung stand.

Sowohl MacArthur als auch die siegreichen Kriegsdienstgegner hielten bis zum Ende durch. Jeder glaubte an seine Sache, MacArthur an die Verwüstung und Zerstörung des Krieges, und die Kriegsdienstgegner an die Erlösung und den Frieden eines völlig hingegebenen Lebens. Sie gleichen einander hier lediglich in der Tatsache, dass sie beide kämpften. Der entscheidende Unterschied liegt darin, wofür sie kämpften und wie sie dafür kämpften.

This hymn is generally thought to be one of the most loved hymns written during the latter part of the 19th century. The writing of this thoughtful and beautifully constructed text is even more amazing when we consider that its author was one who was almost completely blind and who describes the writing of this hymn as the “fruit of much mental suffering,” and “the quickest bit of work I ever did in my life.”

Born in Glasgow, Scotland, March 27, 1842, George Matheson had only partial vision as a boy, and, after entering Glasgow University, his eyesight continued to fail rapidly. Except for “moments of shadowy eyesight”, he was totally blind by the age of 18. This affliction of blindness seemed to be a tragedy since he was an eager and avid scholar, yet it caused him to trust in the Lord, and it strengthened his walk with God.

He entered the university at the early age of 15 and graduated with high honors in 1861 at the age of 19. He was a brilliant scholar, even spending four more years after graduation in more theological studies, all the while remaining single. After his graduation he became entirely dependent on others, relying much upon his two sisters, who were so dedicated that they learned Latin, Greek, and Hebrew since they thought it might aid him in his theological studies. One of them continued to be his faithful co-worker and helper throughout his life, assisting in his calling of being a pastor and other ministerial duties.

After completing his theological course, he became assistant pastor to the renowned Dr. Macduff, in whose church of thousands of members he had been brought up. Soon, however, he was chosen minister of the Church of Scotland in the seaport summer resort of Innellan. Here he stayed for eighteen years. Many families came to spend the summer there chiefly to be inspired by his preaching ministry.

Whenever he preached, the open Bible was before him as he stood in the pulpit, and to the congregation, he seemed to be reading from it. During the messages, his eyes looked straight at the congregation, and many went away with no clue that they just listened to a blind preacher. It was during this time that he made a practice of memorizing his sermons, as well as the passages of Scripture he used in his messages. His memory was so sharp that if someone read one of his prepared sermons to him twice, or whatever else he wanted to memorize, he could from then on repeat it perfectly. One Sunday, however, after doing this for 12 years, when in the middle of a powerful sermon his memory completely collapsed, and the topic on which he was preaching vanished from his mind. He sat down and commenced to request a psalm to be sung, and, after the song, with perfect calmness told the audience what had happened. With this done, he stood to his feet, gave out a new text, and preached an impromptu sermon of great power. After that experience George wrote little of his sermons, and finally prepared only an outline from which to preach.

Dr. Matheson’s final pastorate was taken up in 1886 at the age of 44 where he became pastor of the large St. Bernard’s Parish Church in Edinburgh, where his eloquent preaching consistently attracted large throngs of people to the services. Here he remained for 13 years, his church growing from 1,494 members to 1,703 in the first 5 years. He continued faithfully preaching the gospel and became well known as one of Scotland’s outstanding preachers and pastors and was greatly esteemed in Edinburgh where he resided.

Many speculations have been made regarding the cause of the mental distress which prompted the author to write this text. A very popular account, although never verified, is that this text was a result of the severe trial Matheson faced after his soon-to-be bride left him just before their marriage when she learned of his impending total blindness. Although this story cannot be documented, there are many significant hints in this hymn reflecting a saddened heart, such as the “flickering torch” and the “borrowed ray” in the second verse, the tracing of the “rainbow through the rain” in the third stanza, as well as the “cross” in the last verse.

Fortunately, Dr. Matheson did relate an account of his writing of this hymn:

“My hymn was composed in the manse of Innellan on the evening of June 6, 1882. I was at that time alone. It was the day of my sister’s wedding, and the rest of the family were staying overnight in Glasgow. Something happened to me, which was known only to myself, and which caused me the most severe mental suffering. The hymn was the fruit of that suffering and was the quickest bit of work I ever did in my life. A genuine inspiration, I had the impression rather of having it dictated to me by some inward voice than of working it out myself. I am quite sure that the whole work was completed in five minutes and equally sure it never received at my hands any retouching or correction. I have no natural gift of rhythm. All the other verses I have ever written are manufactured articles; this came like a dayspring from on high. I have never been able to gain once more the same fervor in verse.”

The hymn first appeared in the Church of Scotland monthly magazine, Life and Work, in January 1883. The tune was composed one year later by a prominent Scotch organist of his day, Albert L. Peace, who was asked to write a tune especially for Matheson’s text.

Peace’s own account of the writing of this fine tune is as follows, “After reading it over carefully, I wrote the music straight off, and may say that the ink of the first note was hardly dry when I had finished the tune.” The origin or the tune name, St. Margaret, is unknown except that it is a name much revered in Scotland, and certainly because of the beloved Queen Margaret of Scotland.

The later years of Matheson’s life from the age of 57 to his death at age 64 were spent in writing some of the finest devotional writings in the English tongue, including Moments on the Mount, Voice of the Spirit, and Rests by the River. Although this is his only hymn found in most hymnals, he did write a few other fine hymns, including “Make Me A Captive Lord”, and “Then I Shall Be Free.”

The four key words of “O Love, That Wilt Not Let Me Go” are: love, light, joy, and cross. These words have been described as the complete satisfaction for any believer whose life is totally surrendered to the will of God. It could take the rest of one’s life to completely discover the personal significance of these four expressions.

Composer       -Albert L. Peace, 1844 – 1912

Este himno suele considerarse uno de los más queridos compuestos durante la segunda mitad del siglo XIX. La redacción de este texto reflexivo y bellamente construido resulta aún más asombrosa si consideramos que su autor era casi completamente ciego y que describió la escritura de este himno como el “fruto de mucho sufrimiento mental” y “el trabajo más rápido que he hecho en mi vida”.

Nacido en Glasgow, Escocia, el 27 de marzo de 1842, George Matheson tenía visión parcial de niño y, después de ingresar en la Universidad de Glasgow, su vista siguió fallando rápidamente. Excepto por “momentos de vista sombría”, quedó totalmente ciego a los 18 años. Esta aflicción de ceguera pareció una tragedia ya que era un estudioso entusiasta y ávido, pero le llevó a confiar en el Señor y fortaleció su caminar con Dios.

Ingresó en la universidad a la temprana edad de 15 años y se graduó con altas calificaciones en 1861, a los 19 años. Fue un brillante erudito, incluso pasando cuatro años más después de la graduación en estudios teológicos, todo el tiempo permaneciendo soltero. Tras su graduación se volvió totalmente dependiente de otros, confiando mucho en sus dos hermanas, que estaban tan dedicadas que aprendieron latín, griego y hebreo porque pensaban que podrían ayudarle en sus estudios teológicos. Una de ellas continuó siendo su fiel colaboradora y ayudante a lo largo de su vida, auxiliándole en su ministerio pastoral y otras labores ministeriales.

Tras completar su curso teológico, se convirtió en pastor asistente del renombrado Dr. Macduff, en cuya iglesia de miles de miembros se había criado. Pronto, sin embargo, fue elegido ministro de la Iglesia de Escocia en la estación veraniega portuaria de Innellan. Allí permaneció dieciocho años. Muchas familias venían a pasar el verano allí principalmente para inspirarse con su ministerio de predicación.

Siempre que predicaba, la Biblia abierta estaba delante de él mientras se levantaba en el púlpito, y para la congregación parecía estar leyéndola. Durante los mensajes, sus ojos miraban directamente a la congregación, y muchos se marchaban sin sospechar que acababan de escuchar a un predicador ciego. Fue durante este tiempo que tomó la costumbre de memorizar sus sermones, así como los pasajes de las Escrituras que usaba en sus mensajes. Su memoria era tan aguda que si alguien le leía uno de sus sermones preparados dos veces, o cualquier otra cosa que quisiera memorizar, desde entonces podía repetirlo perfectamente. Un domingo, sin embargo, después de hacer esto durante 12 años, en medio de un poderoso sermón su memoria se vino completamente abajo y el tema sobre el que predicaba desapareció de su mente. Se sentó y comenzó a pedir que se cantara un salmo y, después del canto, con perfecta calma contó a la audiencia lo que había ocurrido. Con esto hecho, se puso de pie, dio un nuevo texto y predicó un sermón improvisado de gran poder. Después de esa experiencia George escribió poco de sus sermones y finalmente sólo preparaba un bosquejo del cual predicar.

El pastorado final del Dr. Matheson comenzó en 1886, a los 44 años, cuando se hizo pastor de la gran iglesia parroquial de St. Bernard’s en Edimburgo, donde su elocuente predicación atraía constantemente a grandes multitudes a los servicios. Allí permaneció durante 13 años, creciendo su iglesia de 1.494 miembros a 1.703 en los primeros 5 años. Continuó predicando fielmente el evangelio y llegó a ser conocido como uno de los predicadores y pastores más destacados de Escocia, y fue muy estimado en Edimburgo, donde residía.

Se han hecho muchas especulaciones sobre la causa de la angustia mental que motivó al autor a escribir este texto. Un relato muy popular, aunque nunca verificado, afirma que este texto fue resultado de la dura prueba que enfrentó Matheson después de que su prometida lo dejara poco antes del matrimonio al enterarse de su inminente ceguera total. Aunque esta historia no puede documentarse, hay muchos indicios significativos en este himno que reflejan un corazón entristecido, como la “antorcha parpadeante” y el “rayo prestado” en la segunda estrofa, el trazar el “arco iris a través de la lluvia” en la tercera estrofa, así como la “cruz” en la última estrofa.

Por fortuna, el Dr. Matheson relató un relato sobre la composición de este himno:

“Mi himno fue compuesto en la casa parroquial de Innellan en la noche del 6 de junio de 1882. En aquel momento estaba solo. Era el día de la boda de mi hermana y el resto de la familia se quedó esa noche en Glasgow. Me sucedió algo que sólo yo conocía y que me causó el más severo sufrimiento mental. El himno fue el fruto de ese sufrimiento y fue el trabajo más rápido que he hecho en mi vida. Una inspiración genuina; tuve más bien la impresión de que me fue dictado por alguna voz interior que de que yo lo hubiese elaborado. Estoy bastante seguro de que toda la obra se completó en cinco minutos y con la misma seguridad de que nunca recibió de mi mano retoque ni corrección. No tengo don natural para el ritmo. Todas las demás estrofas que he escrito son artículos manufacturados; esta vino como un amanecer desde lo alto. Nunca he podido recuperar esa misma fervor en verso.”

El himno apareció por primera vez en la revista mensual de la Iglesia de Escocia, Life and Work, en enero de 1883. La melodía fue compuesta un año después por un prominente organista escocés de su tiempo, Albert L. Peace, a quien se le pidió que escribiera una melodía especialmente para el texto de Matheson.

El propio relato de Peace sobre la composición de esta fina melodía es el siguiente: “Después de leerlo detenidamente, escribí la música de un tirón, y puedo decir que la tinta de la primera nota apenas estaba seca cuando terminé la melodía.” El origen del nombre de la melodía, St. Margaret, se desconoce, salvo que es un nombre muy venerado en Escocia, y ciertamente por la querida reina Margaret de Escocia.

Los últimos años de la vida de Matheson, desde los 57 hasta su muerte a los 64, los dedicó a escribir algunos de los más finos escritos devocionales en lengua inglesa, entre ellos Moments on the Mount, Voice of the Spirit y Rests by the River. Aunque éste es su único himno que se encuentra en la mayoría de los himnarios, sí escribió algunos otros himnos notables, entre ellos “Make Me A Captive Lord” y “Then I Shall Be Free”.

Las cuatro palabras clave de “O Love, That Wilt Not Let Me Go” son: amor, luz, gozo y cruz. Estas palabras han sido descritas como la satisfacción completa para cualquier creyente cuya vida esté totalmente rendida a la voluntad de Dios. Podría llevar el resto de la vida descubrir por completo el significado personal de estas cuatro expresiones.

Referencias:

101 Hymn Stories
Treasury of Hymn Stories
Author            -George Matheson, 1842 – 1906
Composer       -Albert L. Peace, 1844 – 1912

Jehoshaphat was in trouble. He had just heard the news that a great multitude was coming to fight against him. At that moment he did what all of us naturally do when a multitude of problems come against us. He was afraid. How well I know the feeling of fear, the dread that grips my heart at times. Sometimes it’s the big things, like being misunderstood and misused, or the fear and pain of sickness, or the death of a loved one. Sometimes it’s small things, like loneliness on a Sunday afternoon. This is not comfortable, God, and I’m afraid.

Jehoshaphat laid his fear aside, set himself to seek the Lord, and proclaimed a fast throughout all the land of Judah – verse 3. Even in this seemingly impossible situation of having thousands of men on their way to destroy him and his people, he fell before the Lord and acknowledged His perfect, omnipotent rule. And [he] said, O LORD God of our fathers, art not thou God in heaven? and rulest not thou over all the kingdoms of the heathen? and in thine hand is there not power and might, so that none is able to withstand thee? –verse 6.

The choice is mine. I wrestle with my own fearful thoughts, turning them over and over in my mind as if hoping to change the situation with my messy and fearful concoctions. Clinging to my fear gives me a feeling of being in control. But it is killing me from the inside out, even without the dreaded “what ifs” becoming reality. Finally, I let go and fall exhausted at my Lord’s feet, and my heart echoes the words of Jehoshaphat, the king of Judah.

In humble entreaty, Jehoshaphat acknowledges their weakness and need for God’s power. O our God, wilt thou not judge them? for we have no might against this great company that cometh against us; neither know we what to do: but our eyes are upon thee. –verse 12.

Yes, God, I am nothing in the grand scheme of things. I have no power, not even to be the fruitful worker in Your kingdom that I always dreamed of being. I can’t fight this battle.

Jehoshaphat realized that he alone, as one man, had no strength. He called all the people of Judah together, And all Judah stood before the LORD, with their little ones, their wives, and their children –verse 13. They knew the strength in unity. As they stood before the Lord, waiting for Him to speak, the Spirit of the Lord came down and God gave them the words of help and hope that they were desperate for.

…Be not afraid nor dismayed by reason of this great multitude; for the battle is not yours, but God’s –verse 15. Often I try to fight my battles inside of myself rather than making myself vulnerable to others. But, as soon as I invite others into my life and into my battles, I find the strength of God through His people. When we are confused and disillusioned, we need the people of God. When we all pray together, we will get an answer to our prayer for direction.

Jehoshaphat heard the next directive from God. Tomorrow go ye down against them … Ye shall not need to fight in this battle: set yourselves, stand ye still, and see the salvation of the LORD … fear not, nor be dismayed; to morrow go out against them: for the LORD will be with you –verses 16-17. These words comfort my heart. Often the easiest thing to do is try to fix things, to quickly come up with a remedy of some sort to get myself out of this dilemma, to try to convince myself that everything will be okay. But God tells my heart to sit still without fear and let Him do the fighting. This takes more spiritual muscle than all the action, all the doing, and all the worrying; plus, it accomplishes a lot more.

And Jehoshaphat bowed his head with his face to the ground: and all Judah and the inhabitants of Jerusalem fell before the LORD, worshipping the LORD –verse 18. If I obey and trust instead of worry and sit still instead of jumping into the middle of things, then I will see God do miracles. No, not always in changing my circumstances or removing all the hard things, but He does a miracle in my own soul which changes my focus and attitude. And that causes me to worship because it’s a miracle which only the all-mighty, all-powerful God can do.

Do you think any of them slept that night? They knew a fearsome army was on its way to destroy them and yet… they had heard God speak. Just perhaps there was a joyful expectation in their hearts and an eager anticipation to see how God was going to win this battle. When I learn to practice trust in the little things and the big things that pile into my life, I will soon learn to have a heart of excited expectation, because I know He is going to do something! He is going to give me a way out. Even if the worst happens, He will show my heart the way of peace and He has promised to be with me through it all. And after all, the ultimate victory is already won, so what do all these infractions really have to do with my peace and joy? Nothing.

Morning dawned; it was the day God had told them to go out against these enemies. They arose with no delay. They all knew obedience was paramount in receiving God’s blessing that day. And as they went out of the city, Jehoshaphat exhorted them. And they rose early in the morning, …and as they went forth, Jehoshaphat stood and said, …Believe in the LORD your God, so shall ye be established; believe his prophets, so shall ye prosper. And… he appointed singers unto the LORD, and that should praise the beauty of holiness, as they went out before the army… – verses 21-20. He appointed singers to sing as they went, proclaiming to everyone and to the opposing army that they were on the Lord’s side.

I would have liked to see that huge army going out of the city, singing. They were facing a daunting task and one that would have made the strongest man tremble, but they were singing. And when they began to sing and to praise, the LORD set… [an ambush] against the children of Ammon, [and] Moab, …which were come against Judah; and they were smitten …every one helped to destroy another –verses 22-23.

The people of Judah went to their watch tower and in amazement saw that their enemies had destroyed each other, and they saw nothing but an army of dead bodies. When a fearsome battle is set in array against me, I can still make the decision to trust and sing. Singing is a deliberate act of worship; it reminds our own souls and the souls of everyone listening that the Lord, He is God. He is the One in complete charge of my circumstances, of my tiny world, and all its problems. Suddenly the enemies are dead. The circumstances may not have changed, but the battle is finished in my soul.

The army of Judah spent the next three days gathering the riches and spoils from the dead bodies of their enemies, collecting so much that they couldn’t carry it all away with them. Astonishing! But that is how it is every time. My spirit benefits from the hard things that I endure successfully. Each victory allows me to collect ‘spoils’ which will profit me for the rest of my life. My heart is full of blessing, of being cared for, and being carried by a Heavenly Father. The “armies of Moab and Ammon” have brought blessing instead of ruin.

They came again to their homes in Jerusalem with singing, and harps, and trumpets, overloaded with all their spoil. The fear of God fell on all the kingdoms of the land when they heard how God had fought this huge battle, then Jehoshaphat’s realm was quiet. Peace reigned.

The peace of knowing that all I really need is God and His working in my life is the ultimate peace. This broken world can bring all manner of pain, sickness, and disappointments, but God brings rest to the heart that was once so full of tumult and fear. There is rest ‘round about’ and all the ‘kingdoms of the land’ will be amazed and curious at the strength that is within us, because it is the strength that no one can match—the strength of our amazing God.

约沙法遇到了麻烦。他刚听到有一大批人要来攻击他。那一刻，他做了我们在遭遇众多问题时自然会做的事。他害怕。我多么熟悉那种害怕的感觉，那种有时会攫取我心的惶恐。有时是重大的事，比如被误解和被利用，或疾病带来的恐惧与疼痛，或至亲的离世。有时则是小事，比如周日下午的孤独。这并不舒服，神啊，我很害怕。

约沙法把恐惧放到一边，决心寻求耶和华，并在犹大全地宣告禁食——第3节。 即便在这种看似不可能的情形中，有成千上万的人正要来灭他和他的子民，他仍俯伏在主面前，承认祂完美、全能的统治。于是他说、耶和华我们父神阿、你不在天上作神么、你不管列国么、在你手中岂没有能力大能、无人能敌挡你么？——第6节。

选择在我。我与自己惶恐的思绪搏斗，一遍遍在心里翻来覆去，仿佛希望靠自己杂乱而恐惧的臆想来改变处境。紧抓着恐惧让我有一种掌控感。但它正从内里吞噬我，即便那些可怕的“假如”并未成真。终于，我放手，精疲力竭地伏在主脚前，心里回响着犹大的王约沙法的话。

约沙法以谦卑的恳求承认他们的软弱并需要神的大能。我们的神阿、你岂不审判他们么、因为我们无力抵挡这来攻击我们的众多、我们也不知道当作何事、惟有仰望你。——第12节。

是的，神啊，在宏观安排中我算不得什么。我没有能力，甚至无法成为你国里我曾梦想成为的那位多结果的工人。我打不赢这场仗。

约沙法明白他单靠一人之力是没有力量的。他召聚了所有犹大人，犹大全体都站在耶和华面前、连幼小的、妻子、儿女也站在耶和华面前——第13节。他们知道合一的力量。当他们站在主面前，等待祂说话时，耶和华的灵降下，神赐给他们那些他们迫切需要的帮助与盼望的话。

……不要因这众多的人惊恐害怕、因为争战不是你们的、乃是神的——第15节。 我常在内心与自己的争战，而不是向他人敞开自己。但我一旦邀请别人进入我的生命和争战，就能通过祂的子民找到神的力量。当我们困惑、失望时，我们需要神的子民。当我们一同祷告，我们就会得到方向的回答。

约沙法听见神接下来的指示。明日你们下去迎敌……这争战不是你们要打的、要站住、静观耶和华的拯救……不要惧怕、也不要惊惶、明日你们出去迎敌、因为耶和华必与你们同在——第16–17节。这些话安慰我的心。常常最容易做的事是试图修补事情，迅速想出某种补救法来把自己从困境中拉出来，试图说服自己一切都会好。然而神对我的心说，要无惧地静坐，任由祂去争战。这比所有的行动、所有的作为和所有的忧虑都需要更多属灵的力量；而且，这样做成就更多。

约沙法便俯伏面于地、犹大众人、并耶路撒冷的居民、都俯伏敬拜耶和华——第18节。 若我选择顺服并信靠而非忧虑，静坐而非匆忙投入事端，我就会看见神行奇事。不，不总是改变外在处境或消除所有艰难，但祂在我心里行一件奇事，改变我的焦点和态度。那会引我进入敬拜，因为唯有全能的神才能行这样的奇事。

你认为他们那夜有人睡着吗？他们知道有一支凶猛的军队要来毁灭他们，然而……他们听见了神的话。也许他们心中有喜乐的盼望，热切期待看神如何赢得这场仗。当我学会在生活的大大小小事上练习信靠，我很快就会学会拥有一颗兴奋期待的心，因为我知道祂必做些事！祂要给我出路。即便最坏的事情发生，祂也会向我心显明平安的道路，并应许与我同在经历这一切。毕竟，最终的胜利已经成就，这些过犯与我的平安喜乐又有什么关系呢？没有关系。

晨光升起；那是神叫他们出来迎敌的日子。他们毫不耽搁地起来。他们都明白顺服在那天领受神的赐福上至关重要。他们出城的时候，约沙法激励他们。次日他们清晨起来……他们出去的时候、约沙法站着说、——你们当信耶和华你们的神、就必得坚立、也当信他的先知、就必亨通。并且……他为耶和华设立歌唱的人、他要称赞圣者的美、在军前行唱——第20–21节。他打发歌唱的人去行进，在军队前赞美，向众人以及敌军宣告他们是站在主一边的。

我多想看那庞大的军队出城时一边唱歌。他们面对的是令人生畏的任务，足以使最强壮的人颤抖，但他们仍在歌唱。他们一面唱歌、一面称赞的时候、耶和华在亚捫人、摩押人、并来攻击犹大的人身上设伏兵、使他们相互攻击、各人击杀邻舍——第22–23节。

犹大人上到望楼去，惊讶地看见他们的仇敌互相残杀，只见一堆一堆的尸首。当一场可怕的争战向我摆阵时，我仍可以决定信靠并歌唱。歌唱是刻意的敬拜行为；它提醒我们自己的灵和所有听者的灵，主就是神。祂完全掌管我的处境，我那小小的世界和其中的一切问题。忽然间，仇敌败亡。外在情况也许未必改变，但争战在我心里已然结束。

犹大军用了接下来的三天将仇敌的财物与掳物聚集起来，收得太多以致无法一次带走。令人惊讶！但每一次都是如此。我历经艰难得胜，我的灵因之受益。每一次胜利都让我得着“掳物”，这将使我受益终生。我的心充满祝福，被天父看顾和背负。那“摩押与亚捫的军队”带来了祝福，而不是毁灭。

他们载着掳物带着歌声、琴瑟与号角回到耶路撒冷的家中，满载而归。列国众民听见神怎样打这场大仗，就都以惧怕临到，那时约沙法的国得以安静。平安掌权。

知道我所真正需要的就是神和祂在我生命中的作为，这就是最终的平安。这个破碎的世界可以带来各种痛苦、疾病与失望，但神给那曾充满骚动与惧怕的心带来安息。“四围”有安息，“地上的列国”都要惊奇并来探问我们里面的力量，因为这是无人能及的力量——我们奇妙神的力量。

Jehoshaphat was in trouble. He had just heard the news that a great multitude was coming to fight against him. At that moment he did what all of us naturally do when a multitude of problems come against us. He was afraid. How well I know the feeling of fear, the dread that grips my heart at times. Sometimes it’s the big things, like being misunderstood and misused, or the fear and pain of sickness, or the death of a loved one. Sometimes it’s small things, like loneliness on a Sunday afternoon. This is not comfortable, God, and I’m afraid.

Jehoshaphat laid his fear aside, set himself to seek the Lord, and proclaimed a fast throughout all the land of Judah – verse 3. Even in this seemingly impossible situation of having thousands of men on their way to destroy him and his people, he fell before the Lord and acknowledged His perfect, omnipotent rule. And [he] said, O LORD God of our fathers, art not thou God in heaven? and rulest not thou over all the kingdoms of the heathen? and in thine hand is there not power and might, so that none is able to withstand thee? –verse 6.

The choice is mine. I wrestle with my own fearful thoughts, turning them over and over in my mind as if hoping to change the situation with my messy and fearful concoctions. Clinging to my fear gives me a feeling of being in control. But it is killing me from the inside out, even without the dreaded “what ifs” becoming reality. Finally, I let go and fall exhausted at my Lord’s feet, and my heart echoes the words of Jehoshaphat, the king of Judah.

In humble entreaty, Jehoshaphat acknowledges their weakness and need for God’s power. O our God, wilt thou not judge them? for we have no might against this great company that cometh against us; neither know we what to do: but our eyes are upon thee. –verse 12.

Yes, God, I am nothing in the grand scheme of things. I have no power, not even to be the fruitful worker in Your kingdom that I always dreamed of being. I can’t fight this battle.

Jehoshaphat realized that he alone, as one man, had no strength. He called all the people of Judah together, And all Judah stood before the LORD, with their little ones, their wives, and their children –verse 13. They knew the strength in unity. As they stood before the Lord, waiting for Him to speak, the Spirit of the Lord came down and God gave them the words of help and hope that they were desperate for.

…Be not afraid nor dismayed by reason of this great multitude; for the battle is not yours, but God’s –verse 15. Often I try to fight my battles inside of myself rather than making myself vulnerable to others. But, as soon as I invite others into my life and into my battles, I find the strength of God through His people. When we are confused and disillusioned, we need the people of God. When we all pray together, we will get an answer to our prayer for direction.

Jehoshaphat heard the next directive from God. Tomorrow go ye down against them … Ye shall not need to fight in this battle: set yourselves, stand ye still, and see the salvation of the LORD … fear not, nor be dismayed; to morrow go out against them: for the LORD will be with you –verses 16-17. These words comfort my heart. Often the easiest thing to do is try to fix things, to quickly come up with a remedy of some sort to get myself out of this dilemma, to try to convince myself that everything will be okay. But God tells my heart to sit still without fear and let Him do the fighting. This takes more spiritual muscle than all the action, all the doing, and all the worrying; plus, it accomplishes a lot more.

And Jehoshaphat bowed his head with his face to the ground: and all Judah and the inhabitants of Jerusalem fell before the LORD, worshipping the LORD –verse 18. If I obey and trust instead of worry and sit still instead of jumping into the middle of things, then I will see God do miracles. No, not always in changing my circumstances or removing all the hard things, but He does a miracle in my own soul which changes my focus and attitude. And that causes me to worship because it’s a miracle which only the all-mighty, all-powerful God can do.

Do you think any of them slept that night? They knew a fearsome army was on its way to destroy them and yet… they had heard God speak. Just perhaps there was a joyful expectation in their hearts and an eager anticipation to see how God was going to win this battle. When I learn to practice trust in the little things and the big things that pile into my life, I will soon learn to have a heart of excited expectation, because I know He is going to do something! He is going to give me a way out. Even if the worst happens, He will show my heart the way of peace and He has promised to be with me through it all. And after all, the ultimate victory is already won, so what do all these infractions really have to do with my peace and joy? Nothing.

Morning dawned; it was the day God had told them to go out against these enemies. They arose with no delay. They all knew obedience was paramount in receiving God’s blessing that day. And as they went out of the city, Jehoshaphat exhorted them. And they rose early in the morning, …and as they went forth, Jehoshaphat stood and said, …Believe in the LORD your God, so shall ye be established; believe his prophets, so shall ye prosper. And… he appointed singers unto the LORD, and that should praise the beauty of holiness, as they went out before the army… – verses 21-20. He appointed singers to sing as they went, proclaiming to everyone and to the opposing army that they were on the Lord’s side.

I would have liked to see that huge army going out of the city, singing. They were facing a daunting task and one that would have made the strongest man tremble, but they were singing. And when they began to sing and to praise, the LORD set… [an ambush] against the children of Ammon, [and] Moab, …which were come against Judah; and they were smitten …every one helped to destroy another –verses 22-23.

The people of Judah went to their watch tower and in amazement saw that their enemies had destroyed each other, and they saw nothing but an army of dead bodies. When a fearsome battle is set in array against me, I can still make the decision to trust and sing. Singing is a deliberate act of worship; it reminds our own souls and the souls of everyone listening that the Lord, He is God. He is the One in complete charge of my circumstances, of my tiny world, and all its problems. Suddenly the enemies are dead. The circumstances may not have changed, but the battle is finished in my soul.

The army of Judah spent the next three days gathering the riches and spoils from the dead bodies of their enemies, collecting so much that they couldn’t carry it all away with them. Astonishing! But that is how it is every time. My spirit benefits from the hard things that I endure successfully. Each victory allows me to collect ‘spoils’ which will profit me for the rest of my life. My heart is full of blessing, of being cared for, and being carried by a Heavenly Father. The “armies of Moab and Ammon” have brought blessing instead of ruin.

They came again to their homes in Jerusalem with singing, and harps, and trumpets, overloaded with all their spoil. The fear of God fell on all the kingdoms of the land when they heard how God had fought this huge battle, then Jehoshaphat’s realm was quiet. Peace reigned.

The peace of knowing that all I really need is God and His working in my life is the ultimate peace. This broken world can bring all manner of pain, sickness, and disappointments, but God brings rest to the heart that was once so full of tumult and fear. There is rest ‘round about’ and all the ‘kingdoms of the land’ will be amazed and curious at the strength that is within us, because it is the strength that no one can match—the strength of our amazing God.

جوشافات كان في ورطة. لقد سمع للتو الخبر أن جمعًا عظيمًا قادم ليقاتله. في تلك اللحظة فعل ما نفعله جميعًا بطبيعتنا عندما تواجهنا جموع من المشكلات. خاف. كم أعرف شعور الخوف جيدًا، الرهبة التي تمسك بقلبِي أحيانًا. أحيانًا تكون الأشياء الكبيرة، مثل أن يُساء فهمي ويُستغل، أو خوف وألم المرض، أو موت أحد الأحبة. وأحيانًا تكون أمورًا صغيرة، مثل الشعور بالوحدة في يوم أحد بعد الظهر. هذا ليس مريحًا، يا الله، وأنا خائف.

جوشافات وضع خوفه جانبًا، وجعل نفسه يطلب الرب، وأُعلن صوم في جميع أرض يهوذا – آية 3. حتى في هذا الوضع الذي يبدو مستحيلًا بوجود آلاف الرجال في طريقهم لتحطيمه وتحطيم شعبه، خرَّ أمام الرب واعترف بسيادته الكاملة وقدرته الكلية. وقال: يا رب إِلَه آبائنا، أما أنتَ إِلَه في السموات؟ أما أنتَ لا تملك سلطانًا على جميع ملوك الأمم؟ أليس في يدك القوة والبطش، فلا يستطيع أحد الصمود أمامك؟ – آية 6.

الخيار لي. أنا أصارع أفكاري الخائفة، أُقلبها مرارًا وتكرارًا في ذهني كما لو كنت آمل أن أغير الوضع بخليطتي الفوضوية والخائفة. التشبث بخوفي يمنحني شعورًا بالتحكم. لكنه يقتلني من الداخل، حتى من دون أن تتحقق «ماذا لو» المرعبة. أخيرًا، أترك الأمور وأسقط مرهقًا عند قدمي ربي، وخاطري يردد كلمات جوشافات، ملك يهوذا.

بتضرع متواضع، اعترف جوشافات بضعفهم وحاجتهم لقوة الله. يا إِلَهَنَا، أما أنتَ لا تدينهم؟ لأن ليست لدينا قوة أمام هذا الجمع العظيم الآتي علينا؛ ولا نعلم ما نفعل، لكن أعيننا عليك. – آية 12.

نعم، يا الله، أنا لا شيء في المخطط الكبير للأشياء. ليست لدي قوة، ولا حتى لأكون العامل المثمر في ملكوتك الذي حلمت دائمًا أن أكونه. لا أستطيع خوض هذه المعركة.

أدرك جوشافات أنه بمفرده، كرجل واحد، لا يملك قوة. جمع كل شعب يهوذا معًا، وقام كل يهوذا أمام الرب، مع صغارهم ونسائهم وأولادهم – آية 13. عرفوا قوة الوحدة. وبينما وقفوا أمام الرب منتظرين أن يتكلم، نزل عليهم روح الرب وأعطاهم الله كلمات العون والأمل التي كانوا يائسين منها.

…لا تخافوا ولا ترتعبوا من أجل هذا الجمع العظيم؛ لأن ليس الحرب لكم بل للّه – آية 15. كثيرًا ما أحاول أن أقاتل معاركي داخل نفسي بدل أن أجعل نفسي معرضة للآخرين. لكن بمجرد أن أدعو الآخرين إلى حياتي وإلى معاركي، أجد قوة الله من خلال شعبه. عندما نكون محتارّين ومحبطين، نحتاج إلى شعب الله. عندما نصلي معًا جميعًا، سننال إجابة على صلاتنا لطلب التوجيه.

سمع جوشافات الإرشاد التالي من الله. غدًا اخرجوا عليهم … لن تحتاجوا أن تقاتلوا في هذه المعركة، قِفوا مكانكم، وانظروا خلاص الرب … لا تخافوا ولا ترتعبوا؛ اخرجوا غدًا ضدهم: لأن الرب معكم – آيات 16-17. هذه الكلمات تواسي قلبي. غالبًا أسهل شيء هو محاولة إصلاح الأمور، بسرعة التوصل إلى علاج من نوع ما لإخراجي من هذا المأزق، محاولًا إقناع نفسي بأن كل شيء سيكون على ما يرام. لكن الله يقول لقلبي أن يجلس ساكنًا بلا خوف ويترك له القتال. هذا يتطلب عضلة روحية أكثر من كل الحركة وكل الفعل وكل القلق؛ وفوق ذلك، ينجز الكثير.

وجوشافات خرَّ برأسه نحو الأرض: فخرَّ كل يهوذا وسكان أورشليم أمام الرب، يسجدون للرب – آية 18. إذا أطعت وثقت بدل أن تقلق وجلست ساكنًا بدل أن تقفز إلى وسط الأمور، فسأرى الله يصنع معجزات. لا، ليس دائمًا بتغيير ظروفي أو إزالة كل الصعوبات، لكنه يصنع معجزة في نفسي تغير تركيزي ومواقفي. وهذا يجعلني أسبِّح لأنه معجزة لا يستطيع فعلها سوى الإله القادر الكلي القدرة.

هل تظن أن أحدهم نام تلك الليلة؟ كانوا يعلمون أن جيشًا رهيبًا في طريقه ليفنوا بهم ومع ذلك… لقد سمعوا كلام الله. ربما كان هناك توقع فرح في قلوبهم وترقُّب نشيط لرؤية كيف سيفوز الله بهذه المعركة. عندما أتعلم أن أتمرن على الثقة في الأشياء الصغيرة والكبيرة التي تتكدس في حياتي، سأتعلم سريعًا أن أمتلك قلب توقع مفعم بالحماسة، لأنني أعلم أنه سيفعل شيئًا! سيعطيني مخرجًا. حتى لو حدث الأسوأ، سيُظهر لقلبي طريق السلام وقد وعد أن يكون معي طوال ذلك. وفي نهاية المطاف، النصر الأسمى قد تحقق بالفعل، فماذا تعني كل هذه الإخفاقات لسلامي وفرحي؟ لا شيء.

أشرقت الصباح؛ كان اليوم الذي قال لهم الله أن يخرجوا فيه ضد هؤلاء الأعداء. قاموا بلا تردد. كلهم عرفوا أن الطاعة كانت أمرًا أساسيًا لنيل بركة الله ذلك اليوم. وبينما خرجوا من المدينة، حثَّهم جوشافات. فقاموا باكرًا في الصباح… وبينما كانوا يخرجون قال جوشافات: …آمنوا بالرب إلهكم فتنثبتوا؛ وآمنوا بأنبيائه فتنالوا النجاح. و… عيَّن مطربين للرب ليُمجدوا جلال القداسة، وهم يخرجون أمام الجيش… – آيات 21-20. عيَّن مطربين ليغنوا وهم يخرجون، معلنين للجميع وللجيش المعارض أنهم إلى جانب الرب.

كنت أود أن أرى ذلك الجيش العظيم وهو يخرج من المدينة وهو يغني. كانوا يواجهون مهمة شاقة كانت لتجعل أقوى الرجال يرتعشون، ولكنهم كانوا يغنون. فلما ابتدأوا بالترنيم والتسبيح، أوقع الرب عليهم… [كمينًا] على بني عمون وموآب …الذين جاؤوا ضد يهوذا؛ فهُزموا …وأخذ كل واحد يعين على هلاك صاحبه – آيات 22-23.

صعد شعب يهوذا إلى برج المراقبة وبدهشة رأوا أن أعداءهم قد هلك بعضهم بعضًا، ولم يروا إلا جيشًا من الجثث. عندما تُنصب ضربة مخيفة ضدي، يمكنني مع ذلك أن أختار أن أثق وأغني. الغناء فعل عبادة مقصود؛ يذكر نفوسنا ونفوس كل من يستمع أن الرب، هو الإله. هو المتحكم الكامل في ظروفي، في عالمي الصغير، وكل مشكلاته. فجأة يصبح الأعداء موتى. قد لا تكون الظروف قد تغيرت، لكن المعركة قد انتهت في نفسي.

This hymn is generally thought to be one of the most loved hymns written during the latter part of the 19th century. The writing of this thoughtful and beautifully constructed text is even more amazing when we consider that its author was one who was almost completely blind and who describes the writing of this hymn as the “fruit of much mental suffering,” and “the quickest bit of work I ever did in my life.”

Born in Glasgow, Scotland, March 27, 1842, George Matheson had only partial vision as a boy, and, after entering Glasgow University, his eyesight continued to fail rapidly. Except for “moments of shadowy eyesight”, he was totally blind by the age of 18. This affliction of blindness seemed to be a tragedy since he was an eager and avid scholar, yet it caused him to trust in the Lord, and it strengthened his walk with God.

He entered the university at the early age of 15 and graduated with high honors in 1861 at the age of 19. He was a brilliant scholar, even spending four more years after graduation in more theological studies, all the while remaining single. After his graduation he became entirely dependent on others, relying much upon his two sisters, who were so dedicated that they learned Latin, Greek, and Hebrew since they thought it might aid him in his theological studies. One of them continued to be his faithful co-worker and helper throughout his life, assisting in his calling of being a pastor and other ministerial duties.

After completing his theological course, he became assistant pastor to the renowned Dr. Macduff, in whose church of thousands of members he had been brought up. Soon, however, he was chosen minister of the Church of Scotland in the seaport summer resort of Innellan. Here he stayed for eighteen years. Many families came to spend the summer there chiefly to be inspired by his preaching ministry.

Whenever he preached, the open Bible was before him as he stood in the pulpit, and to the congregation, he seemed to be reading from it. During the messages, his eyes looked straight at the congregation, and many went away with no clue that they just listened to a blind preacher. It was during this time that he made a practice of memorizing his sermons, as well as the passages of Scripture he used in his messages. His memory was so sharp that if someone read one of his prepared sermons to him twice, or whatever else he wanted to memorize, he could from then on repeat it perfectly. One Sunday, however, after doing this for 12 years, when in the middle of a powerful sermon his memory completely collapsed, and the topic on which he was preaching vanished from his mind. He sat down and commenced to request a psalm to be sung, and, after the song, with perfect calmness told the audience what had happened. With this done, he stood to his feet, gave out a new text, and preached an impromptu sermon of great power. After that experience George wrote little of his sermons, and finally prepared only an outline from which to preach.

Dr. Matheson’s final pastorate was taken up in 1886 at the age of 44 where he became pastor of the large St. Bernard’s Parish Church in Edinburgh, where his eloquent preaching consistently attracted large throngs of people to the services. Here he remained for 13 years, his church growing from 1,494 members to 1,703 in the first 5 years. He continued faithfully preaching the gospel and became well known as one of Scotland’s outstanding preachers and pastors and was greatly esteemed in Edinburgh where he resided.

Many speculations have been made regarding the cause of the mental distress which prompted the author to write this text. A very popular account, although never verified, is that this text was a result of the severe trial Matheson faced after his soon-to-be bride left him just before their marriage when she learned of his impending total blindness. Although this story cannot be documented, there are many significant hints in this hymn reflecting a saddened heart, such as the “flickering torch” and the “borrowed ray” in the second verse, the tracing of the “rainbow through the rain” in the third stanza, as well as the “cross” in the last verse.

Fortunately, Dr. Matheson did relate an account of his writing of this hymn:

“My hymn was composed in the manse of Innellan on the evening of June 6, 1882. I was at that time alone. It was the day of my sister’s wedding, and the rest of the family were staying overnight in Glasgow. Something happened to me, which was known only to myself, and which caused me the most severe mental suffering. The hymn was the fruit of that suffering and was the quickest bit of work I ever did in my life. A genuine inspiration, I had the impression rather of having it dictated to me by some inward voice than of working it out myself. I am quite sure that the whole work was completed in five minutes and equally sure it never received at my hands any retouching or correction. I have no natural gift of rhythm. All the other verses I have ever written are manufactured articles; this came like a dayspring from on high. I have never been able to gain once more the same fervor in verse.”

The hymn first appeared in the Church of Scotland monthly magazine, Life and Work, in January 1883. The tune was composed one year later by a prominent Scotch organist of his day, Albert L. Peace, who was asked to write a tune especially for Matheson’s text.

Peace’s own account of the writing of this fine tune is as follows, “After reading it over carefully, I wrote the music straight off, and may say that the ink of the first note was hardly dry when I had finished the tune.” The origin or the tune name, St. Margaret, is unknown except that it is a name much revered in Scotland, and certainly because of the beloved Queen Margaret of Scotland.

The later years of Matheson’s life from the age of 57 to his death at age 64 were spent in writing some of the finest devotional writings in the English tongue, including Moments on the Mount, Voice of the Spirit, and Rests by the River. Although this is his only hymn found in most hymnals, he did write a few other fine hymns, including “Make Me A Captive Lord”, and “Then I Shall Be Free.”

The four key words of “O Love, That Wilt Not Let Me Go” are: love, light, joy, and cross. These words have been described as the complete satisfaction for any believer whose life is totally surrendered to the will of God. It could take the rest of one’s life to completely discover the personal significance of these four expressions.

Este hino é geralmente considerado um dos hinos mais amados escritos durante a última parte do século XIX. A composição deste texto cuidadoso e belamente construído é ainda mais impressionante quando consideramos que seu autor era alguém quase completamente cego e que descreveu a escrita deste hino como o “fruto de grande sofrimento mental” e “o trabalho mais rápido que já fiz em minha vida”.

Nascido em Glasgow, Escócia, em 27 de março de 1842, George Matheson teve visão apenas parcial quando menino e, após ingressar na Universidade de Glasgow, sua visão continuou a falhar rapidamente. Exceto por “momentos de visão sombria”, ficou totalmente cego aos 18 anos. Essa aflição da cegueira parecia ser uma tragédia, pois ele era um estudioso ávido e entusiasmado; contudo, isso o levou a confiar no Senhor e fortaleceu sua caminhada com Deus.

Ingressou na universidade ainda muito jovem, aos 15 anos, e graduou-se com altas honras em 1861, aos 19 anos. Foi um erudito brilhante, passando ainda quatro anos após a formatura em mais estudos teológicos, permanecendo solteiro durante todo esse período. Após a graduação tornou-se inteiramente dependente de outros, contando muito com suas duas irmãs, que se dedicaram tanto que aprenderam latim, grego e hebraico, pois pensavam que isso poderia ajudá‑lo em seus estudos teológicos. Uma delas continuou sendo sua fiel colaboradora e ajudante ao longo de sua vida, auxiliando‑o em seu ministério pastoral e em outras funções ministeriais.

Após concluir o curso teológico, tornou‑se pastor assistente do renomado Dr. Macduff, na igreja do qual, com milhares de membros, ele havia sido criado. Logo, porém, foi escolhido ministro da Igreja da Escócia no balneário portuário de Innellan. Ali permaneceu por dezoito anos. Muitas famílias vinham passar o verão ali principalmente para se inspirarem em seu ministério de pregação.

Sempre que pregava, a Bíblia aberta estava diante dele enquanto permanecia no púlpito, e para a congregação parecia estar lendo dela. Durante as mensagens, seus olhos pareciam mirar diretamente a congregação, e muitos iam embora sem perceber que haviam ouvido a um pregador cego. Foi nesse período que passou a prática de memorizar seus sermões, bem como as passagens das Escrituras que usava em suas mensagens. Sua memória era tão aguçada que, se alguém lhe lesse um de seus sermões preparados duas vezes, ou qualquer outra coisa que quisesse memorizar, ele poderia repeti‑lo perfeitamente dali em diante. Numa ocasião de domingo, entretanto, depois de fazer isso por 12 anos, no meio de um sermão poderoso sua memória colapsou completamente, e o tema sobre o qual estava pregando desapareceu de sua mente. Ele se sentou e pediu que se cantasse um salmo e, depois do canto, com perfeita calma contou ao público o que havia acontecido. Feito isso, levantou‑se, deu um novo texto e pregou um sermão improvisado de grande poder. Após essa experiência, George passou a escrever pouco de seus sermões e, finalmente, preparava apenas um esboço do qual pregava.

O último pastorado do Dr. Matheson começou em 1886, aos 44 anos, quando se tornou pastor da grande St. Bernard’s Parish Church, em Edimburgo, onde sua pregação eloquente atraía consistentemente grandes multidões aos cultos. Ali permaneceu por 13 anos, sua igreja crescendo de 1.494 membros para 1.703 nos primeiros cinco anos. Continuou pregando fielmente o evangelho e tornou‑se conhecido como um dos mais destacados pregadores e pastores da Escócia, sendo muito estimado em Edimburgo, onde residia.

Muitas especulações foram feitas quanto à causa do sofrimento mental que levou o autor a escrever este texto. Um relato muito popular, embora nunca verificado, é o de que este texto foi resultado da severa provação que Matheson enfrentou depois que sua noiva o deixou pouco antes do casamento, ao saber de sua cegueira iminente. Embora essa história não possa ser documentada, há muitas pistas significativas neste hino que refletem um coração entristecido, como a “tocha vacilante” e o “clarão emprestado” no segundo verso, o rastrear do “arco‑íris através da chuva” na terceira estrofe, assim como a “cruz” no último verso.

Felizmente, o Dr. Matheson relatou um episódio sobre a composição deste hino:

“Meu hino foi composto na casa paroquial de Innellan na noite de 6 de junho de 1882. Eu estava então sozinho. Foi o dia do casamento de minha irmã, e o resto da família passou a noite em Glasgow. Algo aconteceu comigo, que só a mim era conhecido, e que me causou o mais severo sofrimento mental. O hino foi o fruto desse sofrimento e foi o trabalho mais rápido que já fiz em minha vida. Uma inspiração genuína; tive mais a impressão de tê‑lo sido ditado por alguma voz interior do que de tê‑lo elaborado eu mesmo. Tenho certeza de que a obra toda foi completada em cinco minutos e igualmente certo de que nunca recebeu de minhas mãos qualquer retoque ou correção. Não possuo dom natural para o ritmo. Todos os outros versos que já escrevi são artigos fabricados; este veio como um amanhecer do alto. Nunca mais consegui recuperar a mesma fervura em verso.”

O hino apareceu pela primeira vez na revista mensal da Igreja da Escócia, Life and Work, em janeiro de 1883. A melodia foi composta um ano depois por um destacado organista escocês de seu tempo, Albert L. Peace, a quem foi pedido que escrevesse uma melodia especialmente para o texto de Matheson.

O próprio relato de Peace sobre a composição desta bela melodia é o seguinte: “Depois de lê‑la cuidadosamente, escrevi a música de imediato e posso dizer que a tinta da primeira nota mal estava seca quando terminei a melodia.” A origem do nome da melodia, St. Margaret, é desconhecida, exceto por ser um nome muito reverenciado na Escócia, e certamente por causa da querida rainha Margaret da Escócia.

Os últimos anos da vida de Matheson, dos 57 anos até sua morte aos 64, foram dedicados à escrita de alguns dos mais finos escritos devocionais em língua inglesa, incluindo Moments on the Mount, Voice of the Spirit e Rests by the River. Embora este seja o único hino seu encontrado na maioria dos hinários, ele escreveu também alguns outros bons hinos, incluindo “Make Me A Captive Lord” e “Then I Shall Be Free”.

As quatro palavras‑chave de “O Love, That Wilt Not Let Me Go” são: amor, luz, alegria e cruz. Essas palavras têm sido descritas como a satisfação completa para qualquer crente cuja vida esteja totalmente entregue à vontade de Deus. Poderia levar o resto da vida de alguém para descobrir completamente o significado pessoal dessas quatro expressões.

Referências:

101 Hymn Stories
Treasury of Hymn Stories
Autor            -George Matheson, 1842 – 1906
Compositor       -Albert L. Peace, 1844 – 1912

All the other verses I have ever written are manufactured articles; this came like a dayspring from on high. I have never been able to gain once more the same fervor in verse.”

The hymn first appeared in the Church of Scotland monthly magazine, Life and Work, in January 1883. The tune was composed one year later by a prominent Scotch organist of his day, Albert L. Peace, who was asked to write a tune especially for Matheson’s text.

Peace’s own account of the writing of this fine tune is as follows, “After reading it over carefully, I wrote the music straight off, and may say that the ink of the first note was hardly dry when I had finished the tune.” The origin or the tune name, St. Margaret, is unknown except that it is a name much revered in Scotland, and certainly because of the beloved Queen Margaret of Scotland.

The later years of Matheson’s life from the age of 57 to his death at age 64 were spent in writing some of the finest devotional writings in the English tongue, including Moments on the Mount, Voice of the Spirit, and Rests by the River. Although this is his only hymn found in most hymnals, he did write a few other fine hymns, including “Make Me A Captive Lord”, and “Then I Shall Be Free.”

The four key words of “O Love, That Wilt Not Let Me Go” are: love, light, joy, and cross. These words have been described as the complete satisfaction for any believer whose life is totally surrendered to the will of God. It could take the rest of one’s life to completely discover the personal significance of these four expressions.

References:

101 Hymn Stories
Treasury of Hymn Stories
Author            -George Matheson, 1842 – 1906
Composer       -Albert L. Peace, 1844 – 1912

המזמור הזה נחשב בדרך כלל לאחד מהמזמורים האהובים שנכתבו בשלהי המאה ה־19. הכתיבה של הטקסט המחושב והמנוסח להפליא הזה מרשימה עוד יותר כששוקלים שמחברה היה אדם שעיוור כמעט לגמרי ותיאר את כתיבת המזמור כ"פרי סבל נפשי רב", וכ"העבודה המהירה ביותר שעשיתי אי־פעם בחיי".

נולד בגלזגו שבסקוטלנד ב־27 במרץ 1842, ג'ורג' מת'יסון ראה רק חלקית בילדותו, ולאחר שנכנס לאוניברסיטת גלזגו המשיכה ראייתו להדרדר במהירות. למעט "רגעים של ראייה צללית", הוא היה עיוור לחלוטין בגיל 18. המכה של העיוורון נראתה כטרגדיה שכן הוא היה מלומד נלהב ותאב דעת, אך היא גרמה לו לבטוח באדון וחיזקה את דרכו עם האל.

הוא נכנס לאוניברסיטה בגיל מוקדם — 15 — וסיים בה בהצטיינות ב־1861 בגיל 19. הוא היה מלומד מבריק, ובמשך ארבע שנים נוספות אחרי הסיום המשיך בלימודים תאולוגיים, כל הזמן נשאר רווק. לאחר סיום לימודיו נהיה תלוי לחלוטין באחרים, כשהוא מסתמך רבות על שתי אחיותיו, שהיו מסורות כל כך עד שלמדו לטינית, יוונית ועברית כי חשבו שזה עשוי לעזור לו בלימודיו התאולוגיים. אחת מהן המשיכה להיות שותפתו הנאמנה והמסייעת לכל אורך חייו, מסייעת בקריאתו להיות פַּסטוֹר ובמטלות משרתיות אחרות.

לאחר שסיים את הקורס התאולוגי הפך לעוזר־מורה לידו של הד״ר מקדאף, בכנסייה שבה גדל, כנסייה שרבתיה היו אלפים. זמן קצר לאחר מכן נבחר למשרת מיני בפרסביטריית הכנסייה של סקוטלנד בעיירת הנופש הימית אינלן. כאן נשאר שמונה־עשר שנים. משפחות רבות הגיעו לבלות את הקיץ שם בעיקר כדי להתעורר ולחוש השראה מתורתו.

Jehoshaphat was in trouble. He had just heard the news that a great multitude was coming to fight against him. At that moment he did what all of us naturally do when a multitude of problems come against us. He was afraid. How well I know the feeling of fear, the dread that grips my heart at times. Sometimes it’s the big things, like being misunderstood and misused, or the fear and pain of sickness, or the death of a loved one. Sometimes it’s small things, like loneliness on a Sunday afternoon. This is not comfortable, God, and I’m afraid.

Jehoshaphat laid his fear aside, set himself to seek the Lord, and proclaimed a fast throughout all the land of Judah – verse 3. Even in this seemingly impossible situation of having thousands of men on their way to destroy him and his people, he fell before the Lord and acknowledged His perfect, omnipotent rule. And [he] said, O LORD God of our fathers, art not thou God in heaven? and rulest not thou over all the kingdoms of the heathen? and in thine hand is there not power and might, so that none is able to withstand thee? –verse 6.

The choice is mine. I wrestle with my own fearful thoughts, turning them over and over in my mind as if hoping to change the situation with my messy and fearful concoctions. Clinging to my fear gives me a feeling of being in control. But it is killing me from the inside out, even without the dreaded “what ifs” becoming reality. Finally, I let go and fall exhausted at my Lord’s feet, and my heart echoes the words of Jehoshaphat, the king of Judah.

In humble entreaty, Jehoshaphat acknowledges their weakness and need for God’s power. O our God, wilt thou not judge them? for we have no might against this great company that cometh against us; neither know we what to do: but our eyes are upon thee. –verse 12.

Yes, God, I am nothing in the grand scheme of things. I have no power, not even to be the fruitful worker in Your kingdom that I always dreamed of being. I can’t fight this battle.

Jehoshaphat realized that he alone, as one man, had no strength. He called all the people of Judah together, And all Judah stood before the LORD, with their little ones, their wives, and their children –verse 13. They knew the strength in unity. As they stood before the Lord, waiting for Him to speak, the Spirit of the Lord came down and God gave them the words of help and hope that they were desperate for.

…Be not afraid nor dismayed by reason of this great multitude; for the battle is not yours, but God’s –verse 15. Often I try to fight my battles inside of myself rather than making myself vulnerable to others. But, as soon as I invite others into my life and into my battles, I find the strength of God through His people. When we are confused and disillusioned, we need the people of God. When we all pray together, we will get an answer to our prayer for direction.

Jehoshaphat heard the next directive from God. Tomorrow go ye down against them … Ye shall not need to fight in this battle: set yourselves, stand ye still, and see the salvation of the LORD … fear not, nor be dismayed; to morrow go out against them: for the LORD will be with you –verses 16-17. These words comfort my heart. Often the easiest thing to do is try to fix things, to quickly come up with a remedy of some sort to get myself out of this dilemma, to try to convince myself that everything will be okay. But God tells my heart to sit still without fear and let Him do the fighting. This takes more spiritual muscle than all the action, all the doing, and all the worrying; plus, it accomplishes a lot more.

And Jehoshaphat bowed his head with his face to the ground: and all Judah and the inhabitants of Jerusalem fell before the LORD, worshipping the LORD –verse 18. If I obey and trust instead of worry and sit still instead of jumping into the middle of things, then I will see God do miracles. No, not always in changing my circumstances or removing all the hard things, but He does a miracle in my own soul which changes my focus and attitude. And that causes me to worship because it’s a miracle which only the all-mighty, all-powerful God can do.

Do you think any of them slept that night? They knew a fearsome army was on its way to destroy them and yet… they had heard God speak. Just perhaps there was a joyful expectation in their hearts and an eager anticipation to see how God was going to win this battle. When I learn to practice trust in the little things and the big things that pile into my life, I will soon learn to have a heart of excited expectation, because I know He is going to do something! He is going to give me a way out. Even if the worst happens, He will show my heart the way of peace and He has promised to be with me through it all. And after all, the ultimate victory is already won, so what do all these infractions really have to do with my peace and joy? Nothing.

Morning dawned; it was the day God had told them to go out against these enemies. They arose with no delay. They all knew obedience was paramount in receiving God’s blessing that day. And as they went out of the city, Jehoshaphat exhorted them. And they rose early in the morning, …and as they went forth, Jehoshaphat stood and said, …Believe in the LORD your God, so shall ye be established; believe his prophets, so shall ye prosper. And… he appointed singers unto the LORD, and that should praise the beauty of holiness, as they went out before the army… – verses 21-20. He appointed singers to sing as they went, proclaiming to everyone and to the opposing army that they were on the Lord’s side.

I would have liked to see that huge army going out of the city, singing. They were facing a daunting task and one that would have made the strongest man tremble, but they were singing. And when they began to sing and to praise, the LORD set… [an ambush] against the children of Ammon, [and] Moab, …which were come against Judah; and they were smitten …every one helped to destroy another –verses 22-23.

The people of Judah went to their watch tower and in amazement saw that their enemies had destroyed each other, and they saw nothing but an army of dead bodies. When a fearsome battle is set in array against me, I can still make the decision to trust and sing. Singing is a deliberate act of worship; it reminds our own souls and the souls of everyone listening that the Lord, He is God. He is the One in complete charge of my circumstances, of my tiny world, and all its problems. Suddenly the enemies are dead. The circumstances may not have changed, but the battle is finished in my soul.

The army of Judah spent the next three days gathering the riches and spoils from the dead bodies of their enemies, collecting so much that they couldn’t carry it all away with them. Astonishing! But that is how it is every time. My spirit benefits from the hard things that I endure successfully. Each victory allows me to collect ‘spoils’ which will profit me for the rest of my life. My heart is full of blessing, of being cared for, and being carried by a Heavenly Father. The “armies of Moab and Ammon” have brought blessing instead of ruin.

They came again to their homes in Jerusalem with singing, and harps, and trumpets, overloaded with all their spoil. The fear of God fell on all the kingdoms of the land when they heard how God had fought this huge battle, then Jehoshaphat’s realm was quiet. Peace reigned.

The peace of knowing that all I really need is God and His working in my life is the ultimate peace. This broken world can bring all manner of pain, sickness, and disappointments, but God brings rest to the heart that was once so full of tumult and fear. There is rest ‘round about’ and all the ‘kingdoms of the land’ will be amazed and curious at the strength that is within us, because it is the strength that no one can match—the strength of our amazing God.
